title: Block close: always possible
hookLine: the laws that began with confession end with love
tomorrow: what happens in the gaps a story leaves out?

cards: The last page of anything gets reread: the final scene of a show, the last text before a friend moved away. These laws of return began with words of confession, out loud: I did this, I regret it, I won't again.
And they end in love: a mind sick with love, a love that grows with knowing. One idea runs between the two ends.

teach.b: The idea is this: return is always possible. The door doesn't shut on age or on a long record.
In chapter two Maimonides writes that even someone who wronged all their days and returned on the day of their death is forgiven. That's the week's question: how does a tradition hold that door open?
And one neighbor holds it open in its own words.
Muslims, too, have a word for it that means return, as teshuvah does: tawbah, from a root meaning to turn back.
And the Qur'an, in Pickthall's translation, says to people who have wronged themselves: "Despair not of the mercy of Allah, Who forgiveth all sins." That's the shared thread.
Two traditions, each with a word that means turning back, each insisting that no one is too far gone to turn. And one honest difference. Maimonides writes as a lawgiver.
He lays out the road: the spoken confession, the repair, the test of the same chance, the commandments with their shape.
The verse in the Qur'an speaks as a call, addressed straight to the person who has gone too far, telling them not to lose hope.

teach.h: ONE BUILDS THE ROAD, ONE CALLS.
teach.b: One builds the road; the other calls down it. Neither is a copy of the other, and neither needs to be.
Thirty days with this law book, and the last word sounds a lot like the first: always possible.

how: Jews return to these laws every year in the month of Elul and the Ten Days of Return before Yom Kippur; Maimonides' Laws of Return is a classic text studied in that season.

o: turning back happens once a year, at Yom Kippur
turning back can happen at any point in life

tawbah, from a root meaning to turn back.
teshuvah and tawbah are one teaching in two languages
they share the turning; Maimonides builds steps, the verse calls not to despair.

games.q: a friend says, 'i've messed up too many times. it's too late for me.' what do both of today's texts say?
o: it's still possible; neither text closes the door.
it depends how many times; there's a limit somewhere.
only if you can undo every single thing first.
games.why: Maimonides: even return on the last day is accepted. the Qur'an: despair not of the mercy of Allah. different voices, the same open door.

practice: If you can, stand, or shift in your seat, and slowly turn your body to face a different direction from the one you were facing. Let that small physical turn be the whole practice: one turn, made on purpose.
Then settle, and breathe in the new direction until the bell.
